Discussion on the interpretation (ta'wil) of His saying, exalted is He:

[1–3] ﴿I swear by this city﴾ ﴿and you are a resident of this city﴾ [al-Balad: 2] ﴿and by the begetter and what he begot﴾ [al-Balad: 3]

﴿I swear by this city﴾: The explanation of "I swear" has already been given in several places of the Noble Revelation. "The city" is Makkah. He qualified the oath with His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and you are a resident of this city﴾ [al-Balad: 2], out of concern for the Prophet, may God's blessings be upon him. It is as if it were an oath by it (Makkah) on his account, with an allusion to the lack of honour of the people of Makkah, and that they were in great ignorance, because of their intention to expel one who is truly deserving of it, and through him its honour is completed.

Al-Shihab said: "Al-hill" (the resident/lawful one) is an adjective of a verbal noun in the sense of the one who alights (al-hall) in this interpretation. There is no weight to those who denied it, because it is not attested in the lexicographical books. It was also said: its meaning is "and you are one whose sanctity is violated in it, and who is exposed to harm." In this there is an expression of wonder at their state in their enmity towards him, and an allusion to their gathering and dispersing, that he is not violated in it even by pigeons; so how would the blood of the guide of mankind, upon him be prayer and peace, be violated in it?

It was also said: its meaning is "and you will be made lawful for it in the future, doing in it whatever you wish of killing and captivity," an indication of what will happen of the conquest of Makkah and its being made lawful for him for an hour of a day, in which he killed and took captives, although it had not been conquered for anyone before him, nor made lawful for anyone; so in this there is consolation for him, a promise of his victory, and the destruction of his enemy. "Al-hill" under these two interpretations is the opposite of "sanctity" (al-hurmah), and in both there is—as they have said—remoteness, especially the intention of the future tense in the last interpretation, for it is not what is readily understood from it. The first was preferable for honouring him, peace be upon him, by making his alighting in it the basis of magnifying him, along with alerting from the outset to the certainty of the content of the answer, by mentioning some sources of plotting, in the manner of (p-6160) the excellence of the opening, and that he endured hardships and encountered the severe trials, in the path of calling to God, that no caller before him had endured, God's blessings and peace be upon him.

﴿and by the begetter and what he begot﴾ [al-Balad: 3]: It is coordinated (ʿatf) upon "this city," included in the thing sworn by. It was said: what is meant is Adam and his offspring; and it was said: Abraham and his offspring. The correct view, as Ibn Jarir said, is that what is meant is every begetter and what he begot. He said: "It is not permissible to restrict that except with a proof that must be accepted, from a report or from reason, and there is no report specifying that, nor any demonstration requiring acceptance of it specifically. So it remains general as it is general."

The use of "mā" (what) rather than "man" (who) is for the intention of description, and it conveys magnification in the context of praise, and that it is of a kind whose reality cannot be fully grasped due to the intensity of its vagueness. For this reason it conveys amazement or the causing of amazement, even if it is not interrogative, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And God knows best what she had given birth to﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 36], meaning: what a child of great status she gave birth to. This is evident if the intended meaning is Abraham and the Prophet, peace be upon them both. As for the view that what is meant is Adam and his offspring, the amazement is at their multitude, or at what man is distinguished by among the special qualities of humankind, such as speech, reason, and beauty of form. Related by al-Shihab.

The Interpretation of His Words, Exalted is He:

[4–7] ﴿Indeed, We created man in toil.﴾ ﴿Does he think that no one will ever have power over him?﴾ [Al-Balad: 5] ﴿He says, "I have squandered wealth in abundance."﴾ [Al-Balad: 6] ﴿Does he think that no one has seen him?﴾ [Al-Balad: 7]

﴿Indeed, We created man in toil.﴾ That is: in hardship. He struggles with affairs and deals with them through all his stages, from his carrying (in the womb) until he settles in his final abode: either in Paradise or in Hell.

Al-Zamakhshari said: "Al-kabad (toil)" is originally derived from your saying, "kabida al-rajul kabadan," so he is "akbad" when his liver (kabid) is afflicted with pain and swells. Its meaning was then extended until it came to be used for every fatigue and hardship, and from it the word "mukabadah" (struggling) is derived. Similarly it is said, "kabatahu" meaning "he destroyed him." Its origin is "kabidahu," when it strikes his liver. Labid said:

"O eye, why did you not weep for Arbad when we rose and the adversaries stood in toil (kabad)?"

That is: in the severity of the matter and the difficulty of the calamity. End of quotation.

In this there is consolation for the Prophet, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, for what he endures from the Quraysh, on the basis that man was not created for ease in this world, and that whoever is greater in rank is more severely afflicted. This is the essence of what they have said.

Al-Qashani said: "In toil" means in struggle and hardship arising from his own self and his desires, or from an inner sickness, corruption of the heart, and thickness of the veil. For in the language, "kabad" is the thickness of the liver, which is the source of the natural power, and its corruption and the veil over the heart and its corruption stem from this power. So the thickness of the liver is borrowed to describe the thickness of the veil over the heart and the sickness of ignorance.

﴿Does he think﴾ [Al-Balad: 5]: that is, due to the thickness of his veil and the sickness of his heart, since he is veiled by nature, ﴿that no one will ever have power over him﴾ [Al-Balad: 5]: that is, that the Resurrection will never occur, and that no one will be able to requite him, subdue him, or overpower him. Yet what he is in of toil is sufficient to awaken him from his heedlessness and to make him acknowledge his helplessness.

﴿He says, "I have squandered wealth in abundance."﴾ [Al-Balad: 6]: that is, much, from "talabbada al-shay'" (it became matted/clustered) when it gathers together. The intended meaning is what he spent for boasting, vanity, and showing off, like their saying, "I have lost so-and-so upon it," when he spends upon it. He shows favour to people through extravagance and wastefulness, and he regards this as a virtue, due to his being veiled from true virtue and his ignorance. Therefore He said: ﴿Does he think that no one has seen him?﴾ [Al-Balad: 7]: that is, does he think that Allah, Exalted is He, has not perceived his inner self and intention, when he spends his wealth for reputation, showing off, and vanity, and not as it ought to be spent in pleasing Allah? This is a vice upon a vice; how then could it be a virtue?

The discussion of the words of God Most High:

[8–16] ﴿Did We not make for him two eyes?﴾ ﴿And a tongue and two lips?﴾ [al-Balad: 9] ﴿And We guided him to the two highways?﴾ [al-Balad: 10] ﴿But he has not attempted the ascent.﴾ [al-Balad: 11] ﴿And what can make you know what the ascent is?﴾ [al-Balad: 12] ﴿It is the freeing of a neck,﴾ [al-Balad: 13] ﴿or feeding on a day of severe hunger,﴾ [al-Balad: 14] ﴿an orphan near of kin,﴾ [al-Balad: 15] ﴿or a needy man in misery.﴾ [al-Balad: 16]

﴿Did We not make for him two eyes?﴾ ﴿And a tongue and two lips?﴾ [al-Balad: 9] Al-Qashani said: That is, did We not bestow upon him the bodily instruments through which he is able to acquire perfection, so that he may see what he takes as a lesson, ask about what he does not know, and speak about it?

And al-Sayyid al-Murtada said: This is a reminder of the blessings of God upon them, and of what He removed of their impediments in their obligations, and of what He graciously bestowed upon them of instruments through which they reach their benefits and ward off harms from themselves, because the need for most religious and worldly benefits is pressing. So the need for two eyes is for seeing, the tongue for speech, and the two lips for holding food and drink and keeping them in the mouth, and for speech as well.

As for His words, ﴿And We guided him to the two highways?﴾ [al-Balad: 10], that is, the path of good and the path of evil. Al-Imam said: The najd is well known as an elevated road, and what is meant by it here is the path of good and the path of evil. He called them two najds to indicate that in each of them there is roughness and difficulty of passage, so evil is not easier than good as is supposed, and to indicate that both are clear and manifest, such that neither of them is hidden from one who travels them. That is, We placed in his nature the ability to distinguish between good and evil, and We set up for him, from his conscience and his intellect, signs that guide him to them. Then We granted him choice, so it is up to him to choose whichever of the two paths he wishes. Thus He who bestowed upon man these instruments and deposited in his inner being those faculties cannot be escaped by man from His power, and nothing of his inner secret can be hidden from Him.

﴿But he has not attempted the ascent.﴾ [al-Balad: 11] That is, he did not give thanks for those great blessings by attempting the ascent. Al-Iqtiham is entering and passing through with intensity and hardship. Al-Aqaba is a rough path on a mountain that is difficult to traverse. It is used metaphorically for what follows, because of the hardship endured in it and the striving against the self.

﴿And what can make you know what the ascent is?﴾ [al-Balad: 12] What has informed you of what the ascent is? The interrogative adds emphasis to its importance and to its lofty station with God.

﴿It is the freeing of a neck,﴾ [al-Balad: 13] That is, its emancipation, or assisting in it and rescuing it from slavery and the bonds of servitude, returning it to the freedom upon which it was created.

﴿or feeding on a day of severe hunger,﴾ [al-Balad: 14] That is, in a time of famine.

﴿an orphan near of kin,﴾ [al-Balad: 15] That is, one of kinship. Al-Sayyid al-Murtada said: This is an exhortation to give precedence, in bestowing favour, to needy relatives over strangers.

He said: It is also possible that in "maqraba" it is not derived from kinship and nearness of relation, but from nearness in the sense of the flank (khasira), so that the meaning is that he feeds from his flank, which has stuck to him from extreme hunger and hardship. The discussion of the interpretation of His words, exalted is He:

[17–18] ﴿Then he was among those who believed and enjoined one another to patience and enjoined one another to compassion﴾ ﴿Those are the companions of the right hand﴾ [al-Balad: 18]

﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾ meaning: in the truth that had come to them. It is conjoined (ʿuṭifa) to the negated element with "lā" (not), which is "iqtaḥama" (he did not attempt the steep path), or to "fakk" (freeing a slave).

"And enjoined one another" meaning: some of them urged others "to patience," meaning: to endure what befell them in the course of calling to the truth. ﴿And enjoined one another to compassion﴾ meaning: to show mercy toward one another, as in His words: ﴿compassionate among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29]. Or it means: to the requirements of His mercy, exalted is He, such as upholding the truth, proclaiming it openly, and doing righteous deeds. ﴿Those are the companions of the right hand﴾ [al-Balad: 18], meaning: the right side, or the direction of the right in which are the happy ones.

Note (tanbīh):

Al-Qashani said: His words, exalted is He, ﴿So he did not attempt the steep path﴾ [al-Balad: 11] and what follows, point to the subduing of the self through the deliberate practice of virtues and the commitment to following their path and acquiring them, until disposition becomes nature. Then he said: Feeding, especially at a time of great need on the part of the one who deserves it, when it is placed in its proper position, is of the category of the virtue of chastity (ʿiffa) (p-6165), indeed it is the best of its kinds. Faith is of the virtue of wisdom (ḥikma) and the noblest and most excellent of its kinds, and it is the faith of knowledge and certainty. Patience through hardships is among the greatest kinds of courage. He placed it after faith because the virtue of courage cannot be attained without certainty. And "compassion" (al-marḥama), meaning mutual mercy and affection, is among the best kinds of justice. Observe how he enumerated the types of the four virtues by which the perfection of the soul is attained. He began with chastity, which is the first of the virtues, and expressed it by its most significant kinds, and its most distinguished trait, which is generosity. Then he introduced faith, which is the root and foundation. He used the word "then" (thumma) to indicate the distance of its rank from the first in elevation and loftiness, and he expressed wisdom by it, because it is the mother of all its levels and kinds.

Then he ordered patience upon it, since it cannot be realized without certainty. He postponed justice, which is its culmination. He sufficed by mentioning compassion, which is an attribute of the All-Merciful, instead of all its other kinds, just as he sufficed by mentioning patience instead of all other kinds of courage.
